title: The funeral
hookLine: eulogy, psalms, and the prayer "God full of mercy"
last: MOURNERS TEAR THEIR CLOTHES, AND BLESS THE TRUE JUDGE.

cards: No flowers on the plain wooden coffin. Folding chairs, a small chapel, people in coats they don't wear often.
A grandson unfolds a sheet of paper and tells a story about fishing that makes the whole room laugh, then go quiet. Someone reads a psalm.

Then the cantor, or a rabbi, or a friend who knows the tune, begins to sing in Hebrew, slow, rising and falling, and in the middle of it comes a name: the name of the person in the coffin, sung out loud.

teach.b: It's El Male Rachamim, God full of mercy. But first the eulogy, the hesped, which you met in your first year with Abraham.
When Sarah dies, Genesis says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her." The rabbis saw a eulogy there.

A hesped is meant to do both: speak about the person, and let people weep. The codes ask the speaker to praise truly, not to invent a saint, because an honest picture honors the dead more than a flattering one.
Psalms are read, and Psalm twenty-three may be among them: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." It's read as company for the road, not as an explanation. Then the prayer.
El Male Rachamim is a short memorial prayer, usually sung.
It calls on God full of mercy, who dwells on high, to give true rest to the soul of the one who has died, beneath the wings of the divine presence, and it names them.
It asks that their soul be bound up in the bond of life. It may be sung again at the grave, and later on days of remembrance.
In the middle of that slow melody, one ordinary name is sung as if it belongs there.
The funeral says out loud, together, that this person mattered, and hands them, by name, to mercy.

how: A Jewish funeral is usually simple: a eulogy (hesped), psalms, and the memorial prayer El Male Rachamim, sung by a cantor or rabbi with the name of the person who died; it is often sung again at the graveside.

o: a psalm of thanks sung at a wedding feast
a sung prayer asking rest for the soul, by name
a prayer only the rabbi says, silently, alone

p: came to mourn for Sarah and weep

s: a good eulogy makes the person sound perfect
the codes ask the speaker to praise truly, not to invent a saint.
El Male Rachamim names the person who died
in the middle of the melody, their name is sung out loud.
the prayer explains why the person died
it asks God full of mercy to give the soul rest beneath the wings of the divine presence.

games.q: you're giving the eulogy for your grandfather, who was kind and also well known for it, stubborn. what do the codes advise?
o: describe him as a flawless saint.
praise him truly, as he was.
games.why: the codes ask the speaker to praise truly, because an honest picture honors the dead more than flattery.

practice: Bring to mind someone grieving now, or who lost someone this year, and picture them in a crowded room after the service.
Think what it would mean simply to sit beside them, no speech, maybe the name of the one they lost said gently, so they hear it again; if you pray, hold that name in your prayer.
And if your own grief ever feels too heavy, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: El Male Rachamim. God full of mercy: the sung memorial prayer that asks rest for the soul and says the person's name. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: God full of mercy, the memorial prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: god full of mercy. A name said with love is never small. See you tomorrow.
